title: Electrolysis
description: Splitting compounds with electricity, in molten salts and solutions.
hero_image_caption: Pass an electric current through an ionic compound and you can force chemistry to run in reverse — pulling elements apart atom by atom.
content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis uses electricity to decompose an ionic compound into its elements. The compound being broken down is called the electrolyte. For electrolysis to work, the ions must be free to move — so the electrolyte must either be molten or dissolved in water (aqueous).

The electrolyte is placed between two electrodes connected to a direct current supply. The cathode is the negative electrode; the anode is the positive electrode.

Key Fact

Cathode = negative electrode → attracts positive ions (cations) → cations gain electrons here (reduction). Anode = positive electrode → attracts negative ions (anions) → anions lose electrons here (oxidation). Memory aid: PANIC — Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Electrolysis of Molten Ionic Compounds

When a pure ionic compound is melted, its ions become free to move. Passing a current through molten lead bromide (\(PbBr_2\)), for example, produces lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode. In general:

  • At the cathode: metal cations are attracted, gain electrons and are deposited as atoms of the metal.
  • At the anode: non-metal anions are attracted, lose electrons and are released as atoms or molecules of the non-metal.

A half-equation shows what happens at one electrode. Electrons are included, represented as \(e^-\).

For molten lead bromide:
Cathode: \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\) (reduction — gain of electrons)
Anode: \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\) (oxidation — loss of electrons)

Key rule: the number of electrons in each half-equation must balance when you add the two half-equations together. Scale one equation by a multiplier if the charges do not match.

Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, there are additional \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions from the water itself. The electrode product therefore depends on which ions are preferentially discharged:

At the cathode: if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced instead of the metal (water's \(H^+\) ions are discharged). If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen (e.g. copper), the metal is deposited.

At the anode: if a halide ion (\(Cl^-\), \(Br^-\)) is present at significant concentration, the halogen is produced (e.g. chlorine gas from sodium chloride solution). If no halide is present, oxygen is produced from the discharge of hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)).

Question: predict the products at each electrode when copper sulfate (\(CuSO_4\)) solution is electrolysed with inert carbon electrodes.

Step 1: Ions present — \(Cu^{2+}\), \(SO_4^{2-}\), \(H^+\) (from water), \(OH^-\) (from water).

Step 2: At cathode — \(Cu^{2+}\) or \(H^+\). Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so \(Cu^{2+}\) is preferentially discharged. Cathode product: copper metal.

Step 3: At anode — \(SO_4^{2-}\) or \(OH^-\). No halide present, so \(OH^-\) is discharged. Anode product: oxygen gas.

Observations: a reddish-brown coating of copper on the cathode; colourless gas (oxygen) at the anode; the blue colour of the solution fades as \(Cu^{2+}\) ions are removed.

Extraction of Aluminium by Electrolysis

Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, yet it is expensive to produce because it sits above carbon in the reactivity series. It cannot be extracted by reduction with carbon, so electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)) is used instead.

Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point, so dissolving it in molten cryolite (sodium aluminium fluoride) lowers the operating temperature dramatically, reducing energy costs. The electrolysis is carried out in large steel cells lined with graphite, which acts as the cathode. Carbon anodes dip into the molten mixture from above.

Key Fact

Aluminium extraction: Al₂O₃ dissolved in molten cryolite. Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (aluminium deposited). Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (oxygen released). Carbon anodes burn away because oxygen reacts with them at high temperature — they must be replaced regularly, adding to costs.

Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series, which means carbon is not reactive enough to reduce aluminium oxide. Even at very high temperatures, the reaction \(Al_2O_3 + C \rightarrow Al + CO_2\) does not proceed as written, because the stronger bond in aluminium oxide is not broken by carbon.

Additionally, there is a common misconception that aluminium 'rusts'. In fact, aluminium reacts quickly with oxygen in the air to form a thin, tightly bonded aluminium oxide layer. Unlike iron rust, this layer is impermeable and protective — it prevents any further oxidation. This self-sealing property is why aluminium appears unreactive in everyday life despite being quite high in the reactivity series.
exam_tip_html: For electrolysis questions, always start by identifying all the ions present in the electrolyte (including H⁺ and OH⁻ from water in aqueous solutions). Then apply the rules for cathode and anode products. For Higher Tier half-equations, make sure electrons appear on the correct side: gained at cathode (reduction), lost at anode (oxidation). Do not say aluminium 'rusts' in any extended-response — use 'forms a protective oxide layer' instead.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electrolysis uses a direct current to decompose an ionic electrolyte. Cations move to the cathode (negative electrode) and are reduced; anions move to the anode (positive electrode) and are oxidised.
  • In aqueous solutions, hydrogen or the metal is produced at the cathode depending on reactivity; halogen or oxygen is produced at the anode depending on whether halide ions are present.
  • Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite. Carbon anodes gradually burn away because oxygen reacts with them and must be replaced regularly.

practice_questions.text:
During electrolysis, where do positive ions (cations) move?
A) To the anode
B) To the cathode
C) They do not move
D) Away from both electrodes
State what is meant by the term 'electrolyte' and explain why it must be molten or dissolved in water for electrolysis to work.
practice_questions.marks: An electrolyte is an ionic compound that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved [1]; it must be molten or dissolved so that the ions are free to move and carry charge [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens at the cathode and at the anode when molten sodium chloride (NaCl) is electrolysed.
practice_questions.marks: Cathode: Na⁺ ions attracted to cathode [1]; gain electrons to form sodium metal [1]. Anode: Cl⁻ ions attracted to anode; lose electrons to form chlorine gas (Cl₂) [1].

practice_questions.text:
A student electrolyses copper sulfate solution using carbon electrodes.
(a) Predict and explain the product at the cathode.
(b) Predict and explain the product at the anode.
Explain your reasoning for each electrode.
practice_questions.marks: (a) Copper is deposited at the cathode [1] because copper is less reactive than hydrogen so Cu²⁺ ions are preferentially discharged [1]. (b) Oxygen is produced at the anode [1] because no halide ions are present so OH⁻ ions are discharged instead [1].

practice_questions.text:
Write the half-equations for the reactions at the cathode and anode during the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃).
(Higher Tier)
For each half-equation, state whether oxidation or reduction occurs and explain why.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al [1]; reduction — gain of electrons [1]. Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ [1]; oxidation — loss of electrons [1]; electrons balance (6 in each when scaled: 2Al³⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Al and 3O²⁻ → 3/2 O₂ + 6e⁻) [1]. Secure: four points. Developing: correct cathode half-equation and states reduction.

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain why aluminium extraction by electrolysis is more expensive than extracting iron by reduction with carbon in a blast furnace. In your answer, refer to the role of cryolite, the behaviour of the carbon anodes, and the energy requirements of each process.
practice_questions.marks: StudyVault Mastering: aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series so cannot be extracted with carbon [1]; electrolysis requires large, continuous amounts of electrical energy [1]; aluminium oxide has a very high melting point [1]; cryolite is used to dissolve Al₂O₃ and lower the operating temperature, reducing energy costs somewhat [1]; carbon anodes burn away because oxygen reacts with them at high temperature [1]; they must be replaced regularly, adding to maintenance and material costs [1]. Secure: four well-explained points. Developing: identifies electrolysis used and mentions high energy cost.

knowledge_checks.q: What happens at the cathode during electrolysis?
Why is cryolite used in the extraction of aluminium?
options: It reacts with aluminium to purify it
It dissolves aluminium oxide, lowering the melting point
It provides the carbon needed for reduction
It produces aluminium directly by reacting with the ore

knowledge_checks.q: When sodium chloride solution is electrolysed, which gas is produced at the anode: _____
In electrolysis, which electrode is the anode: _____
options: The electrode where metal is deposited
knowledge_checks.explanation: The correct answer is The positive electrode.

knowledge_checks.instruction: Match each term or concept to its correct description
left: What happens at the cathode during electrolysis
cryolite used in the extraction of aluminium
When sodium chloride solution is electrolysed, ...
In electrolysis, which electrode is the anode
right: It dissolves aluminium oxide, lowering the melting point
knowledge_checks.explanation: Review the key terms and definitions covered in this lesson.

flashcard_questions.a: The process of using a direct electric current to break down an ionic compound (electrolyte) into its elements. The electrolyte must be molten or dissolved so ions can move.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a half-equation in electrolysis?
flashcard_questions.a: An equation showing the electron transfer at one electrode. Electrons appear on the left at the cathode (reduction) and on the right at the anode (oxidation).

flashcard_questions.q: Why is cryolite used in the industrial extraction of aluminium?
flashcard_questions.a: It dissolves aluminium oxide, greatly lowering the melting point of the mixture and reducing the energy cost of maintaining the process.

flashcard_questions.q: What determines whether hydrogen or a metal is produced at the cathode in aqueous electrolysis?
flashcard_questions.a: The metal's position in the reactivity series. If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced. If less reactive, the metal is deposited.

flashcard_questions.q: What is produced at the anode when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed?
flashcard_questions.a: Chlorine gas — the chloride ions (Cl⁻) are discharged in preference to hydroxide ions when halide concentration is sufficient.

flashcard_questions.q: Write the half-equation for aluminium production at the cathode.
Why is electrolysis used to extract aluminium rather than reduction with carbon?
flashcard_questions.a: Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon is not reactive enough to displace it from its oxide.

glossary_terms.definition: The process of using a direct electric current to break down an ionic compound (electrolyte) into its elements. The compound must be molten or dissolved so its ions can move freely.
An ionic compound that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water, because its ions are free to move and carry charge.
The negative electrode in electrolysis. Positive ions (cations) are attracted to it and gain electrons here (reduction).
The positive electrode in electrolysis. Negative ions (anions) are attracted to it and lose electrons here (oxidation).
An equation showing the electron transfer at one electrode during electrolysis. Electrons appear on the left for cathode reactions (reduction) and on the right for anode reactions (oxidation).
Al₂O₃, the ore from which aluminium is extracted by electrolysis. It is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower its melting point and reduce energy costs.
A mineral (sodium aluminium fluoride, Na₃AlF₆) used to dissolve aluminium oxide in the industrial extraction of aluminium, significantly lowering the operating temperature.
An ion formed from a halogen atom (Cl⁻, Br⁻, F⁻, I⁻). In electrolysis of aqueous solutions, halide ions at significant concentration are discharged at the anode in preference to hydroxide ions.
